title: Pointers and Box<T>
summary: What a pointer is, references versus smart pointers, raw memory addresses, storing data on the heap with Box, recursive types like the cons list, and how Box sizes them.

blocks.md:
A **pointer** is a variable that holds a memory address: it "points at" some other data. *Rust in Action* puts it plainly: a pointer is an integer that refers to a location in memory, and the type system decides what you may do with it.

Rust has three families:

- **References** (`&T`, `&mut T`) borrow; the borrow checker guarantees they are valid. They have no other abilities and no overhead.
- **Smart pointers** are structs that act like pointers but **own** the data they point to and carry extra behavior. `String` and `Vec<T>` are smart pointers: they own heap memory and know its capacity.
- **Raw pointers** (`*const T`, `*mut T`) are addresses with no guarantees, used in `unsafe` code (chapter 20).

blocks.explain: On a 64-bit machine every plain reference is 8 bytes, whatever it points to. A slice reference is a **fat pointer**: an address plus a length. The real addresses change every run, so this example only compares them; print `{:p}` to see one.

blocks.title: Recursive types
blocks.md: A value of a **recursive type** contains another value of the same type. The classic example is a **cons list**, from Lisp: each item holds a value and the rest of the list, ending with `Nil`. A first attempt does not compile:

blocks.output:
error[E0072]: recursive type `List` has infinite size
 --> src/main.rs:1:1
  |
1 | enum List {
  | ^^^^^^^^^
2 |     Cons(i32, List),
  |               ---- recursive without indirection
  |
help: insert some indirection (e.g., a `Box`, `Rc`, or `&`) to break the cycle
  |
2 |     Cons(i32, Box<List>),
  |               ++++    +

blocks.title: Why the size is infinite, and how Box fixes it

steps.title: Rust sizes an enum by its largest variant
steps.md: For `enum Message { Quit, Move { x: i32, y: i32 }, ... }` it looks at each variant and takes the biggest. That works because each variant has a known size.

steps.title: A List contains a List
steps.md: To size `Cons(i32, List)`, Rust needs the size of `List`, which needs the size of `Cons`, which needs `List`... The computation never ends.

steps.title: A Box has a fixed size
steps.md: `Box<List>` is a pointer: 8 bytes whatever it points to. Now `Cons` is an `i32` plus a pointer, and the next element lives on the heap.

steps.title: The list in memory
steps.md: Each `Cons` sits in its own heap allocation, linked by boxes. This **indirection** (storing a pointer instead of the value) is exactly what the help message suggested.

blocks.output:
Cons(1, Cons(2, Cons(3, Nil)))
sum = 6
a List is 16 bytes
blocks.explain: In `sum(rest)`, `rest` is a `&Box<List>`, and it is passed where a `&List` is expected. That automatic conversion is **deref coercion**, the topic of the next lesson. 16 bytes: 4 for the `i32`, 8 for the box, and the rest is alignment and the variant tag (Rust stores `Nil` in the box's null value).

blocks.title: A boxed binary tree
blocks.md: A binary search tree is recursive too: each node may have a left and a right child. `Option<Box<Node>>` means "maybe a child". Finish `insert` (smaller values go left, others right) and `count`.
hints: `if value < node.value { insert(&mut node.left, value) } else { insert(&mut node.right, value) }`

blocks.title: An expression tree
blocks.goal: Model a recursive data type with Box and evaluate it recursively.
blocks.behavior:
`pub enum Expr { Num(f64), Add(Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>), Mul(Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>), Neg(Box<Expr>), Div(Box<Expr>, Box<Expr>) }` is given.
- `pub fn eval(e: &Expr) -> Result<f64, String>`: evaluates; division by zero gives `Err("division by zero")`.
- `pub fn show(e: &Expr) -> String`: fully parenthesized text, e.g. `(1 + (2 * 3))`, `-(4)`, numbers with `{}` formatting.
- `pub fn depth(e: &Expr) -> usize`: a number has depth 1; others are 1 + the deepest child.
- Helper constructors `pub fn num(v: f64) -> Expr`, `pub fn add(a: Expr, b: Expr) -> Expr`, `pub fn mul(a: Expr, b: Expr) -> Expr` that do the boxing.
hints: `Expr::Add(a, b) => Ok(eval(a)? + eval(b)?)`: `a` is a `&Box<Expr>`, which coerces to `&Expr`.
In `Div`, compute the divisor first and return the error if it is `0.0`.
blocks.solution_explain: Every recursive call passes a `&Box<Expr>` where `&Expr` is expected; deref coercion converts it. Interpreters and compilers represent programs with exactly this kind of boxed tree, called an abstract syntax tree.

questions.q: What makes a smart pointer different from a reference?
options: It owns the data it points to and may add behavior
questions.explanation: String and Vec are smart pointers.

questions.q: Why does `enum List { Cons(i32, List), Nil }` not compile?
How big is a `Box<[u8; 1000]>` value itself on a 64-bit machine?
questions.explanation: The array is on the heap; the box is a pointer.

questions.q: When is Box a good choice?
options: Moving large data without copying it
Storing a value of some type that implements a trait
Sharing one value between several owners
A pointer to a large value
A pointer with extra data, like a slice's address plus length

points: Pointers hold addresses; references borrow, smart pointers own, raw pointers are unchecked.
`Box<T>` puts a value on the heap and frees it when the box goes out of scope.
Recursive types need indirection: `Cons(i32, Box<List>)` has a known size.
Boxes also move big data cheaply and hold trait objects.

terms.def: A value holding the memory address of other data.
A struct that acts like a pointer, owns its data, and adds behavior through Deref and Drop.
A smart pointer that owns a value stored on the heap.
A type that contains a value of itself, which needs indirection to have a known size.
A linked list made of nested pairs of a value and the rest of the list.
A pointer that carries extra data, such as a length, besides the address.
